items: Neutral gas constraints rely on the optically thin approximation and a fixed Na I neutral fraction (1 − y = 0.1), with the Na I D doublet unresolved at R ~ 1000; the absence of a partial covering doublet model (τ–Cf degeneracy) likely underestimates systematic uncertainties on N(Na I) and hence Ṁ_out.
The neutral outflow radius is assumed equal to the ionized outflow radius (3 kpc); absorption cannot directly constrain R_out and Ṁ scales linearly with it.
Electron density n_e is assumed (500 cm−3) for ionized mass estimates with ±0.7 dex systematics; [S II]/[O II] diagnostics are too uncertain to constrain n_e directly.
BPT classification is complicated because some lines (e.g., [O III], Hβ) are dominated by outflowing gas rather than the NLR/ISM; this may bias AGN diagnostics and bolometric inferences.
Energetics and momentum budget are not quantitatively compared to the putative AGN luminosity and to SNe-driven expectations; such a comparison would strongly buttress the AGN-driven conclusion.
Coverage fraction (Cf) of absorbing gas is inferred qualitatively (>50%) but is not fit explicitly; assuming Cf = 1 simplifies but can bias N(H I) estimates.
The reliance on polynomial spectral distortion and a global slit-loss correction (~2×) is sensible but could more clearly quantify how this impacts absolute line luminosities and derived masses.
The large uncertainty on [N II] flux and fixed Hα kinematics may bias BPT placement; an explicit sensitivity analysis on the BPT coordinates would help.

Recent JWST-based Na D neutral-outflow studies at z ~ 1–3 (e.g., population-level Blue Jay Na D incidence and mass-loading; post-starburst/quiescent fossil-outflow cases) could be discussed more thoroughly to position this object within emerging trends.
A brief comparison to IFU-based high-z ionized-outflow studies without AGN (e.g., GA-NIFS) would further emphasize why the ionized phase alone often appears inefficient.
Mapping from drug dose/receptor occupancy to model parameters (e.g., Δτi, Δτe, be changes) is qualitative rather than quantitatively calibrated to pharmacodynamics/pharmacokinetics.

NMDA antagonism is modeled solely as a decreased excitatory decay time τe; ketamine’s network effects (e.g., gamma increases, layer-specific actions, disinhibition) can be more complex and circuit-dependent.
The thalamus and thalamocortical loops are not explicitly modeled, despite their known roles in anesthesia- and sleep-related slow oscillations.
Whole-brain analyses use a single (group-average) connectome and one parcellation; robustness across connectomes, atlases, and conduction velocity/delay choices is not assessed.
The SC–FC analysis lacks controls for potential confounds (e.g., motion, arousal fluctuations, global signal regression choices), and the sample size is inconsistently reported (39 vs 26 subjects).
PCI is computed from firing rates rather than forward-modeled EEG/MEG signals; the thresholding and source-entropy normalization are adapted but not validated against sensor-level PCI.
Minor inconsistencies and typos hinder precision (e.g., “N = 104” likely means 10^4 neurons; 39 vs 26 subjects; occasional switch between Te and τe).
Parameter settings that differ across conditions (e.g., vdrive, global coupling) are not always fully justified, making it hard to disentangle mechanism- vs regime-dependent effects.
Limited quantitative comparison to alternative node models and formulations (e.g., Wilson–Cowan, Hopf, adaptive linear–nonlinear mean-field) regarding robustness of the inferred mechanisms.

Empirical literature indicating potentially distinct PCI effects among anesthetics (e.g., dissociative ketamine vs GABAergic agents) is not fully reconciled with the model’s finding of no significant differences between anesthetic mechanisms.

PAC estimation can be confounded by non-sinusoidal waveforms and transient events (e.g., spikes), and MI significance thresholds or surrogate/analytic nulls are not systematically applied per contact; this limits interpretability of MI magnitude differences relative to potential spurious PAC.
Referencing scheme (e.g., common average, bipolar) and filtering details are not fully specified; both materially affect HFO and MI estimates and may vary across centers or ages.

The tractography analysis is descriptive and uses population-averaged DWI templates; no statistical test links MI co-growth strength to tract density beyond visualization, thus causal inferences about structure–function coupling remain tentative.

The cohort comprises only epilepsy patients with ILAE 1 outcomes; even with “nonepileptic” site selection, generalizability to healthy development is uncertain, and residual pathology or network-level effects may persist.

Sleep staging is identified via visual selection of slow-wave epochs rather than standardized polysomnographic scoring (N2 vs N3); state heterogeneity (and night-to-night variability) is not quantified.

Sensitivity analyses for detector parameter choices, referencing, artifact rejection, and epoch length are limited; findings (e.g., occipital elevation) show detector dependence in the youngest group.

Sampling bias due to clinically driven electrode coverage is unavoidable; the atlas interpolates within 10 mm, but nonuniform coverage could bias regional developmental slopes without explicit coverage-weighting or sampling maps in the main text.
Inconsistencies between uncorrected and FDR-corrected p-values across sections can confuse interpretation; clearer, uniform reporting of corrected significance would help.
The rationale for prioritizing HIL-based HFO rates (beyond alignment with MI computation) could be more explicitly justified given detector discrepancies.

PAC pitfalls and bispectral alternatives are not directly addressed; leveraging analytic null distributions for MI or comparisons to bispectral estimators would strengthen claims (e.g., Aru et al., 2015; Lozano‑Soldevilla et al., 2017).
External validation against larger multi-center resources (e.g., Omni-iEEG) or independent cohorts is not attempted; even partial validation would support generalizability.
Limited theoretical analysis: lacks a stability/wave-number selection theory linking delays, synaptic time constants, and connectivity to predicted wavelengths and speeds.
LFP modeling is simplified (summed synaptic currents plus post-hoc smoothing), omitting volume conduction, laminar mixing, and biophysics that could influence wave detection/metrics.

Inhibitory/excitatory pathway asymmetries (e.g., different spatial extents, synaptic kinetics, and conduction speeds) are not systematically explored, though these are known to shape cortical dynamics.
Sparse participation is central, yet a quantitative “participation index” (fraction of neurons engaged per wave, distribution over space/time) is not explicitly defined or compared to data.

Correlation analyses rely primarily on spike-spike coherence and a global pairwise metric; distance-dependent noise correlations and count correlations across time windows would strengthen the AI claim under waves.
Model–data comparison for wavelength and speed is described as close, but quantitative goodness-of-fit metrics (e.g., KS distances, likelihood-based fits) are not reported.

Some parameters critically shaping dynamics (synaptic time constants, inhibitory delays vs excitatory, refractory periods) are not front-and-center; clearer parameter tables and sensitivity analyses would help reproducibility.
Boundary conditions and edge-handling are briefly mentioned (outer mm discarded) but their effects on wave statistics are not characterized.

Prior theoretical/simulation literature on traveling waves in spatially extended E/I networks with delays (e.g., Roxin–Brunel–Hansel, Ermentrout/Pinto line, rate/phase-reduced analyses) could be engaged more deeply to situate the contribution.

Recent computational platforms enabling large-scale spiking simulations (e.g., NEST GPU onboard instantiation; differentiable simulators like BrainPy) and spiking ML literature on learnable delays and topography provide relevant context for scalability and broader implications.

Field modeling for stimulation appears simplified: SEEG stimulation is mapped via sensor-to-source proximity/decay rather than full patient-specific FEM/EIT solutions with anisotropic conductivities; TI field computation details are insufficient to assess physical fidelity (e.g., tissue conductivities, boundary conditions, anisotropy, and envelope derivation).

The Epileptor-Stimulation coupling (how E-field modulates “m,” thresholds, and parameter scaling) lacks explicit equations and biophysical justification/calibration against empirical stimulation thresholds or afterdischarge phenomena.
Identifiability of parameters and sensitivity to modeling choices (priors, coupling gains, connectivity uncertainties) are not analyzed.

Validation is largely circular: synthetic ictal data are generated from the same model instantiated with the assumed EZ, and the inversion recovers that EZ. This demonstrates internal consistency but not external validity on real stimulation-induced seizures.

No quantitative comparison to alternative EZ mapping approaches (spectral biomarkers, data-driven inference, or other model-based methods), nor ablations isolating benefits of high-resolution modeling or multimodal inversion.
Robustness analyses (noise, electrode localization errors, montage variation, tractography variability, prior mis-specification) are missing.
No computational performance profile (HMC settings, convergence diagnostics, runtime, scalability) is provided.
Critical mathematical details (Epileptor-Stimulation equation(s), likelihood/data-feature definition, multimodal likelihood fusion) are deferred or absent, making replication difficult.
Minor typographical inconsistencies (e.g., “measial,” “Fl,” “forth”) and figure OCR artifacts impede precision in some places.
Limited engagement with recent advances in TI field modeling and optimization (e.g., FEM-based montage design, safety/SAR constraints) and broader perturbational modeling literature.
No discussion of safety/feasibility bounds (current intensities, envelope thresholds, charge density at SEEG contacts, TI heating/SAR), which are essential for clinical translation.
